abstract: The BLS Employment Situation for September 2026, released October 2, 2026. Nonfarm payrolls rose 29,000 and the unemployment rate was 4.2 percent, both described by BLS as little changed. The release matters to jobsdata.ai as the aggregate check on AI displacement claims: if AI were removing jobs at the scale the louder forecasts imply, it would show here first. This vintage also revised July and August down by a combined 60,000, reversing the upward revisions that the August release had used to erase July's reported payroll loss.
keyFindings: Total nonfarm payroll employment changed little in September (+29,000), following an average monthly gain of 45,000 over the prior 12 months - a decelerating but still positive trend.
Both the unemployment rate, at 4.2 percent, and the number of unemployed people, at 7.1 million, changed little in September.
July was revised down by 31,000, from +21,000 to -10,000, and August down by 29,000, from +162,000 to +133,000; employment in July and August combined is 60,000 lower than previously reported.

Information and professional and business services - the two industries most exposed to generative AI - both appear in the list of major industries that changed little over the month, so neither shows the sharp decline the August vintage recorded for information.
Health care employment continued its upward trend (+17,000) but at a slower pace than its +33,000 prior-12-month average.
Average hourly earnings edged up 5 cents, or 0.1 percent, to $37.81, and are up 3.0 percent over the year - a slower annual pace than the 3.1 percent reported in August.
methodology: Two monthly surveys run for BLS by the Census Bureau: the establishment survey of roughly 119,000 businesses and agencies (payroll employment, hours, earnings) and the household survey of about 60,000 households (unemployment rate, labor force participation). Seasonally adjusted. Payroll estimates are revised in each of the two following releases as more reports arrive, which is why the July figure has now been published three times with three different signs of trend.
qualifiers: An aggregate measure with no AI attribution of any kind. Monthly payroll changes carry sampling error of roughly plus or minus 130,000 at the 90 percent confidence level, so a +29,000 print is statistically indistinguishable from zero and from the 12-month average. The revision history is the stronger caution: the July figure has moved from -23,000 to +21,000 to -10,000 across three vintages, so any AI-displacement reading built on a single month's payroll change is reading noise. Industry lines described as 'little changed' carry no published figure in the narrative text.
